title: Irreducible polynomials with coefficient restrictions
subject: finite-fields
summary: Frobenius orbits count irreducible polynomials over finite fields and give construction algorithms. Prescribed coefficients, allowed coefficient sets, and factorization statistics lead to distinct counting problems.
questionsAnswered: How many monic irreducibles of degree n exist over a finite field?
How does counting yield an exact construction algorithm?
Which arbitrary coefficients can be prescribed simultaneously?
How does restricting every coefficient differ from prescribing selected coefficients?
Why do factor degrees resemble permutation cycles, and in which limit?

sections.title: Counting irreducible polynomials
sections.body:
Let \(N_q(n)\) count monic irreducibles of degree \(n\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), where \(q\) is a prime power. Every element of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) is a root of \(x^{q^m}-x\), whose derivative is \(-1\). A monic irreducible divides this polynomial exactly when its degree divides \(m\).

Derivation

\[q^m=\sum_{d\mid m}dN_q(d),\qquad N_q(n)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)q^{n/d}.\]

The second identity is Möbius inversion; \(\mu\) is the Möbius function. Every proper divisor of \(n\) is at most \(n/2\), giving \(N_q(n)=q^n/n+O(q^{n/2}/n)\), uniformly for \(q\ge2\). Thus a uniform monic polynomial is irreducible with probability asymptotic to \(1/n\) as \(n\to\infty\), even for fixed \(q\).

Example

\[N_2(6)=\frac{64-8-4+2}{6}=9.\]

Thus nine of the 64 monic binary sextics are irreducible. All nine have constant coefficient one, so nine of the 32 constant-one sextics are irreducible.

citations.note: Finite-field structure and irreducible-polynomial counting; the derivation is included explicitly.

sections.title: Construction algorithms
sections.body:
Independent uniform sampling of monic polynomials, followed by the exact Frobenius-power irreducibility test, gives a Las Vegas construction. Sampling continues until the test proves irreducibility; the runtime is random and the output is certified. For binary sextics, sampling only constant-one candidates takes exactly \(32/9\) trials on average.

If an extension \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) is already represented, choose \(\alpha\) outside its maximal proper subfields. Equivalently, require \(\alpha^{q^{n/\ell}}\ne\alpha\) for every prime \(\ell\mid n\). Its minimal polynomial is then \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(x-\alpha^{q^i})\). This construction assumes a representation of the extension field.

Shoup develops deterministic constructions, including bounds polynomial for small characteristic, and faster construction methods. Polynomial dependence on the characteristic \(p\) need not be polynomial in its bit length \(\log p\).

citations.note: Probabilistic finite-field algorithms, with exact irreducibility verification.
Deterministic constructions and dependence on the characteristic.
Faster construction of irreducible polynomials of prescribed degree.

Given \(n\ge2\), \(0\le j

The exceptional cases follow from elementary obstructions: a zero constant term supplies the factor \(x\); in characteristic two, \(x^2+c\) is a square because finite fields are perfect. For \(n\ge3\), the constant-term obstruction is the only one.

Wan proved a large-parameter range and Ham–Mullen finished the remaining cases. Tuxanidy–Wang give another proof: sufficiently long periods of finite-field discrete Fourier transforms force elements of full degree in supports of functions encoding elementary symmetric coefficients. Irreducibility here does not require a root to generate the multiplicative group.

sections.title: Several prescribed coefficients
sections.body:
Let \(I\subset\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) have size \(r\); prescribe arbitrary \(a_i\in\mathbb F_q\), requiring \(a_0\ne0\) if \(0\in I\). Pollack proves, for fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\le(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt n\),

\[\#\{f\text{ irreducible with these coefficients}\}\sim\sigma N_q(n),\quad \sigma=\begin{cases}q^{-r},&0\notin I,\\q^{1-r}/(q-1),&0\in I,\end{cases}\]

as \(n\to\infty\), uniformly in the field and prescriptions.

Theorem (Ha)

For every prime power \(q\), if \(n\ge52\) and \(r\le n/10\), every such prescription is realized by a monic irreducible. Thus any six chosen coefficients of a degree-60 polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) can be prescribed, subject to the constant-term condition.

Ha also obtains \(\lfloor(1/4-\varepsilon)n\rfloor\) prescriptions for \(n\ge8\), \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), and \(q\ge q_0(\varepsilon)\). The proofs use exponential-sum estimates and the function-field circle method, with a positive main term larger than the error. The conclusions apply within the stated ranges for the number of prescribed coefficients.

citations.note: Uniform growing-degree asymptotic, including the constant-coefficient normalization.
Explicit all-fields linear range, large-field quarter-degree range, and proof strategy.

sections.title: Forbidden coefficient values
sections.body:
Prescribing a few coefficients and restricting all coefficients to large sets are different problems. Porritt treats a common forbidden set using the function-field circle method. Cheng allows the forbidden set to depend on the coefficient position.

Theorem · Cheng, fixed field and growing degree

Fix a prime power \(q\ge300\). For each \(0\le i\[\#\mathcal I=\frac{q}{n(q-1)}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}|A_i|\left(\Delta+O\bigl(q^{-\sqrt{n/45}}\bigr)\right),\qquad \Delta=\frac{|A_0\setminus\{0\}|}{|A_0|},\]

for sufficiently large \(n\). The cited theorem gives an explicit threshold. The estimate applies to allowed sets satisfying the stated size condition.

The factor \(\Delta\) removes the constant-zero obstruction. For example, if every coefficient must be nonzero, the count is asymptotic to \(q(q-1)^{n-1}/n\). If each position must avoid a specified value \(c_i\), multiply this main term by \(1\) when \(c_0=0\), and by \((q-2)/(q-1)\) otherwise. These counts apply as the degree tends to infinity.

citations.note: Common forbidden set; q≥500, |R|<√q/2, n≥100(log q)² in the displayed theorem.
Position-dependent forbidden sets, exact constant-term factor, and explicit sufficient threshold.

sections.title: Square coefficients
sections.body:
Theorem · Bary-Soroker–Shmueli, published 2026

Fix \(n\ge1\). Choose the \(n\) nonleading coefficients of a monic degree-\(n\) polynomial independently and uniformly from the set of square values \(S_q=\{u^2:u\in\mathbb F_q\}\), including zero. Then

\[\Pr(f\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb F_q)=\frac1n+O_n(q^{-1/2}),\qquad q\longrightarrow\infty.\]

For odd \(q\), uniform sampling from \(S_q\) differs from squaring a uniform element of \(\mathbb F_q\): the latter gives zero half the weight of each nonzero square. For even \(q\), squaring is a bijection and this is the unrestricted model.

The proof uses finite-field Chebotarev and disjointness of suitable function-field extensions. The paper also handles coefficient sets of bounded algebraic complexity. Its fixed-degree error term does not establish a fixed-field, growing-degree analogue.

Example

Over \(\mathbb F_5\), the square values are \(0,1,4\). The polynomial \(x^2+x+1\) has square coefficients and is irreducible because its discriminant is \(2\), a nonsquare. By contrast, \(x^2+1=(x-2)(x+2)\). Thus square coefficients alone do not imply irreducibility.

citations.locator: Theorem 1; Theorem 2 and §§3–5 for the broader method
citations.note: Monic polynomial, independent uniform square values, fixed n, q→∞; the O-constant depends on n.

sections.title: Factorization statistics
sections.body:
For a partition \(\lambda=1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\) of \(n\), unique factorization gives the exact number of squarefree monic polynomials of type \(\lambda\):

\[\prod_{j=1}^n\binom{N_q(j)}{m_j}\sim\frac{q^n}{z_\lambda},\qquad z_\lambda=\prod_j j^{m_j}m_j!,\qquad q\to\infty\quad(n\text{ fixed}).\]

Indeed, choose the distinct factors of each degree independently. The factor \(1/z_\lambda\) is also the probability of cycle type \(\lambda\) in \(S_n\).

Theorem (Bank–Bary-Soroker–Rosenzweig)

Let \(f\) be monic of degree \(n\) and \(3\le m\[\frac{q^{m+1}}{z_\lambda}+O_n(q^{m+1/2}).\]

The proof identifies \(S_n\) as geometric monodromy of the parameter family and translates Frobenius cycle types into point counts. This group belongs to a function-field cover; an individual finite-field splitting extension still has cyclic Galois group.

Remark

The interval estimate has a constant depending on \(n\); its stated asymptotic fixes \(n\) and lets \(q\to\infty\). It does not establish the corresponding fixed-\(q\), growing-degree assertion. The unrestricted \(1/n\) probability in that regime follows separately from Möbius inversion.

citations.note: Foundational use of function-field Galois groups to study factorization distributions.
Uniform interval estimate for 3≤m<n and its geometric-monodromy proof; smaller m requires extra hypotheses.

related.why: Frobenius-power tests certify the output of construction algorithms.
Cycle types record factor degrees both for arithmetic reduction and for finite-field parameter families.
Extension-field representations and irreducibility testing are basic inputs to factorization algorithms.
Finite-field models distinguish increasing field size from increasing degree; neither is the integer-coefficient model.
The geometric group of a finite-field family can differ from the groups of its specializations.
Sparsity conjectures ask for irreducibles with few nonzero coefficients.

questions.title: Can any one coefficient be prescribed?
questions.scope: Monic degree n≥2 polynomials over every finite field
questions.body: Yes, with exactly the constant-zero and even-characteristic quadratic exceptions stated above. Primitive-polynomial prescriptions are a different problem with additional multiplicative conditions.

questions.title: Which coefficient positions allow stronger bounds?
questions.scope: Fixed finite field, growing degree, and a specified family of prescription patterns
questions.body: For a specified pattern of positions and values, one can ask for a larger proportion of prescribed coefficients, an asymptotic count, or an efficient construction. The bounds above establish sufficient ranges; they need not be optimal or the strongest known for every pattern.

questions.title: Can degree and coefficient restrictions vary simultaneously?
questions.scope: A specified sequence of fields, degrees, and allowed coefficient sets
questions.body: The problem depends on which of \(q,n\) and the sets \(A_i\) vary. Cheng’s theorem allows increasing degree with large allowed sets, whereas the square-coefficient theorem fixes the degree. For a specified model, one can seek estimates uniform in both parameters or compare the ranges of these results. This formulation does not assert that every intermediate regime is open.
